books.section: Topic 4.10 The Second Great Awakening, Transcendentalism

stimulus.text: Ralph Waldo Emerson, "Self-Reliance," 1841: "Trust thyself: every heart vibrates to that iron string. Accept the place the divine providence has found for you, the society of your contemporaries, the connection of events."
stimulus.source_note: Verbatim quotation from Ralph Waldo Emerson, "Self-Reliance," Essays: First Series (1841). Public domain; wording checked against the published text.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: Emerson's main idea in this passage is that individuals should do which of the following?

options.text: Obey the customs of their society without question
options.misconception: Emerson mentions 'the society of your contemporaries,' so it is easy to read that as obedience.

options.text: Trust their own judgment over the expectations of others
Seek wealth through hard work in factories
options.misconception: Self-reliance sounds like getting ahead by work, so it is easy to tie it to wages.

options.text: Leave the United States to study in Europe
options.misconception: Emerson knew European thought well, so it is easy to think he sent readers back to Europe.

rationales.A: Emerson's first words are 'Trust thyself,' the opposite of obeying custom without question.
rationales.B: The iron string is the reader's own heart; Emerson tells the reader to trust it, not the crowd.
rationales.C: The passage says nothing about factories or wealth; its subject is judgment, not wages.
rationales.D: Emerson wanted Americans to stop imitating Europe, not to sail there to study.
rationales.general:
1. Read the first two words. 'Trust thyself' is a command to the reader, not to a crowd.
2. Read the image. A heart vibrating to an iron string means an inner guide, not outside opinion.
Background: 'Self-Reliance' is the best-known statement of transcendentalist self-trust.
Remember: when a passage opens with a command, that command is usually its main idea.
